transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-12
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM), Maya Patel (Astra Head of SRE), Daniel Reyes (Astra CTO), Anika Moore (Astra Platform)

Auto-generated summary: partial available (see summary above)

00:00 Jared: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we've got about an hour. The goal is to walk through the postmortem, confirm root cause, and align on mitigations and next steps. Maya, do you want to kick off with the customer timeline?
00:18 Maya: Yeah thanks Jared. So on 2025-09-09 around 10:12 Pacific we saw the first latency spike in production, token latencies jumped from ~120ms to 700ms and by 10:30 we had increased error rates for a subset of customers. We scaled up the pool but saw degraded throughput and some requests queuing.
00:42 Daniel: Just to add, our traffic had a small burst from a partner job, higher average sequence length, but nothing out of the ordinary. The weird part was that after autoscaler scaled, throughputs didn't return to normal for about 25-30 minutes.
01:05 Priya: So our initial instrumentation shows a burst of KV cache evictions concurrent with small GPU restarts — looks like some backend node churn led to repeated KV cache warmups. That combined with the autoscaler policy which ramped quickly then tried to rebalance, resulted in hot shards moving around. When hot shards moved you had cache misses and higher per-token compute.
01:28 Anika: We did see the hot-node being rebalanced a couple times, and some of our long-running requests were re-routed. There might have been a race between the scheduler and the cache priming.
01:45 Jared: Right. There were also three config differences: Astra is on a slightly smaller batch target, and you have prefix caching disabled on some routes, plus a fairly aggressive default autoscale cooldown.
02:02 Maya: We also noticed our KMS rotations were happening around then, I don't know if it's related but we saw some short-lived auth retries.
02:16 Priya: Auth retries shouldn't cause sustained latency but if combined with repeated cache churn it could worsen the tail. We saw a pattern where the KV cache warmup path invoked more CPU work and that pushed some orchestrator tasks.
02:35 Daniel: Can you clarify KV cash, sorry? I think I heard KV cash.
02:39 Priya: (laughs) yeah sorry transcription; KV cache, it's the key-value attention cache for long-context models. Sometimes it's referred to as KV store.
02:52 Jared: Let's step through the timeline doc — I posted a link in the chat to the incident-timeline.xlsx and the draft postmortem.
03:10 Liam: Quick note on impact: about 8% of calls in that hour got >500ms additional latency; 1.2% error spike; no data exfiltration, nothing hit S3 or external DBs.
03:28 Maya: Correct — the issue was service availability and degraded latency, which for us triggered alerts since our SLA requires p95 < 200ms for critical routes.
03:40 Priya: On root cause we have three working hypotheses: 1) KV cache eviction due to node churn (primary), 2) autoscaler thrash causing hot-shard migration timing issues (contributor), 3) transient KMS auth retries adding orchestration pressure (minor).
04:05 Daniel: Which of those is the smoking gun?
04:09 Priya: Evidence leans toward hypothesis 1 + 2 combined. The node churn logs show three short-lived restarts around 10:15-10:18 that correlate tightly with cache misses and queue growth. The autoscaler then moved capacity around which amplified cache warmup.
04:30 Maya: Why did nodes restart? We saw an OOM on one process, possibly from a quantization path that triggered on a particular model variant.
04:42 Priya: We have a note about a recent model update to v1.4 that introduced a new kernel path. There's a footprint change in some cases; we are still investigating if that's causal.
05:00 Anika: If the model variant increased memory, that could explain the OOM and churn. We did roll that variant to a subset of traffic last week.
05:14 Jared: Ok so short-term mitigations: pin the older model variant for critical routes, enable prefix caching on the critical endpoints, and increase autoscaler cooldown and target counts so we avoid immediate rebalancing. Long-term: Dedicated capacity or hot-shard pinning and additional memory telemetry for kernel paths.
05:35 Daniel: Walk me through Dedicated — would that guarantee the hot shard doesn't move and reduce warmups?
05:42 Priya: Dedicated capacity gives you reserved GPU pools and more control. You can configure shard pinning and avoid Kubernetes-like autoscaler rebalances that can cause warmup. It reduces noisy neighbor and scheduling churn. It's not a silver bullet — you still need to tune cache and priming — but it materially reduces the probability of this particular class of incident.
06:08 Maya: What about cost, and if we wanted to trial Dedicated for two weeks — can we scope a trial that lets us run our peak traffic?
06:20 Jared: Yes, we can provision a trial with sizing guidance. We'll send a cost and config sheet. Goal is to let you exercise the same traffic profile.
06:30 Liam: Also worth considering aggressive KV prefix caching and a manual cache-priming step during deploys. That would reduce the initial cold-start penalty even if you remain on shared capacity.
06:45 Anika: How invasive is prefix caching? Does it change the API or token billing?
06:52 Priya: It's configuration at the route level; it doesn't change billing semantics, just stores common prefixes in the KV store to reduce compute on warm requests. Some routes are safe to enable, others (highly dynamic inputs) are not.
07:10 Daniel: Regarding security, Maya brought up KMS rotation — can you confirm whether the KMS retries could block the runtime and cause backpressure?
07:20 Priya: It shouldn't block the main generation loop; auth failures are retried asynchronously. But if you couple that with large cache warmups and high CPU in coordination tasks, you can get queueing. We'll review the auth retry paths and backoff config.
07:40 Liam: We'll also share SOC2-related audit notes — the incident didn't expose data, but you'll get our audit logs for KMS and RBAC to reassure your security team.
07:55 Maya: Please include the exact span traces we need for our ticketing system so we can map alerts to Redwood spans.
08:05 Priya: We'll export traces and a recommended set of spans to capture around model loading, kv cache hits/misses, and autoscaler events.
08:18 Jared: Ok let's list agreed mitigations and ownership — short-term (next 7 days): pin model variant, enable prefix caching on critical routes, adjust autoscaler cooldown; medium-term (2-4 weeks): Dedicated trial, cache-priming tooling, memory telemetry; long-term (quarter): kernel path regression tests integrated into our model onboarding.
08:45 Maya: Sounds good. For the model pin, who does that?
08:50 Jared: Redwood can rollback the model pin on your behalf; action: Jared will coordinate with Priya to perform the rollback during a maintenance window.
09:02 Priya: We'll also add an alert for cache-miss rate surges so you can get earlier warning than the p95 breach.
09:12 Daniel: Any change to SLAs if we go Dedicated?
09:16 Jared: Dedicated comes with SLA options; we can work with legal. For trial we can provide best-effort elevated support and pre-commit to runbooks.
09:30 Anika: Can you share the postmortem doc link? The chat link is in the meeting — we need that to paste into our ticket.
09:38 Liam: Posted: https://redwood-internal/docs/astra/postmortem-20250909 (draft). Also shared incident-timeline.xlsx and runbook.md in the chat.
09:50 Maya: Great — we'll review and provide comments.
09:56 Jared: Recap of action items and next steps: Priya will reproduce on staging and share traces, Jared sends Dedicated trial proposal, Liam will push KMS logs. We'll schedule the remediation session next week. Anything else?
10:10 Daniel: Please include an outline for the remediation planning session so we can prep.
10:15 Jared: Will do. Thanks everyone.
10:20 meeting end

Notes: transcript contains a few mis-hearings (KV cash -> KV cache), occasional truncated sentences typical of automated transcription. Links referenced in chat: postmortem draft, incident-timeline.xlsx, runbook.md, Dedicated trial proposal (to be sent).
